panels.title: Requests running
panels.description: minisgl_running_requests gauge — in-flight decode batch.

panels.title: Requests waiting (queue)
panels.description: minisgl_waiting_requests gauge — queued, not yet scheduled.

panels.title: Decode speed (tok/s)
panels.description:
Per-stream decode rate = 1 / mean TPOT, measured prefill-excluded as (completion_time - first_token_time) / (tokens - 1).

This is the speed one request's tokens arrive at, not the server's aggregate — see "Token throughput" for that. It records on request COMPLETION, so it lags in-flight generation and stays flat during a long request; on a low request rate it can hold a stale value for minutes.

Use it to answer "how fast does a single user's stream feel?" — it is unaffected by prefill time and by idle gaps between requests.

panels.title: Prompt tok/s
panels.description: Prompt tokens/s actually run through prefill; tokens served from the prefix cache are excluded. Measured over a single 1 s scrape interval (irate) and reported as the peak within each display bucket, so it shows the real burst rate at any zoom level and reads 0 when nothing is prefilling. For the prefill kernel's own rate — computed tokens per GPU-second spent in prefill — see "Prefill throughput (compute)".

panels.title: KV-pool utilization
panels.description: used/total KV-cache token slots.

panels.title: GDN-state utilization
panels.description: used/total GDN recurrent-state slots (hybrid models).

panels.title: Mean accept-len (tok/step)
panels.description: accepted/steps = minisgl_spec_accepted_tokens_total / minisgl_spec_steps_total. Headline lever for DFlash/DDTree speed. (No +1 bonus term — matches the repo's accept-len convention where 0.26 / 1.30 / 2.15 are reported.)

panels.title: Draft acceptance rate
panels.description: accepted/drafted = minisgl_spec_accepted_tokens_total / minisgl_spec_draft_tokens_total.

panels.title: Drafted tok/s
panels.description: Speculative draft tokens proposed per second. Measured over a single 1 s scrape interval (irate), reported as the peak within each display bucket: the rate while drafting is actually running, not an idle-inclusive average.

panels.title: Accepted tok/s
panels.description: Speculative draft tokens accepted by verify, per second. Measured over a single 1 s scrape interval (irate), reported as the peak within each display bucket. Compare against "Drafted tok/s" for the acceptance fraction.

panels.title: Mean accept-len over time
panels.description: accepted/steps over time — watch DFlash/DDTree tuning move this.

panels.title: Draft acceptance rate over time
panels.description: accepted/drafted fraction over time.

panels.title: Token throughput (incl. prefix cache)
panels.description: Generation and prompt token rates. Each series is measured over a single 1 s scrape interval (irate) and plotted as the peak within each display bucket, so a burst keeps its true height however far you zoom out. "prefill cached (saved)" is prompt tokens served from the prefix cache — work skipped, not work done.

panels.title: Requests running / waiting
panels.description:
running = requests currently decoding. queued + prefilling = requests admitted but not yet decoding: either waiting for KV capacity or with a prefill still in flight.

Each point is the PEAK over that interval, not a point sample, so a request shorter than the graph's resolution still shows up when you zoom out. Heights are therefore peaks, not averages — a bucket reading 4 may have averaged 1.

A long prompt sits in "queued + prefilling" for the whole of its prefill and only moves to "running" at its first generated token.

Read together: the second series climbing while the first stays flat means a queue backlog (check KV-pool utilization); both moving together is healthy batching.

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Requests/s arrived, succeeded, and aborted. Measured over a single 1 s scrape interval (irate), peak within each display bucket.

panels.title: Error rate
panels.description: aborted / (success + aborted), clamp_min guards divide-by-zero.

GPU memory bandwidth (GB/s, effective)
panels.description: Effective GDDR6 bandwidth = UMC (memory-controller) activity x peak. Peak = mem_clock_MHz x 0.512e9 B/s (256-bit bus, GDDR6 16n prefetch: 640 GB/s @ ~1250 MHz, auto-tracks the memory OC). Dashed line = peak at the current clock.

panels.title: GPU memory-controller activity (UMC %)
panels.description: amdgpu_umc_activity_percent — measured fraction of time the memory controller is busy (the directly-reported BW-utilization signal the GB/s panel is derived from).

panels.title: CPU busy
panels.description: node_cpu_seconds_total, all cores, non-idle share. Whole-box: every container and host process, not just the serve. Sustained high with low GPU load means the host side is the limiter.

panels.title: CPU iowait
panels.description: Share of CPU time blocked on I/O. Rises when the offload path is reading weights or the PLE table from NVMe faster than it can be served. Compare against the demand-paging panel.

panels.title: RAM used
panels.description: 1 - MemAvailable/MemTotal. MemAvailable already discounts reclaimable page cache, so this is real pressure, not cache. Above ~90% expect allocation stalls and swap.

panels.title: RAM available
panels.description: node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes — what a new allocation can get without swapping, including reclaimable cache. This is the headroom figure to size an offload arena against, not MemFree.

panels.title: Swap used
panels.description: SwapTotal - SwapFree across both swap devices: 45.9 GiB of zram (compressed RAM, priority 100, filled first) and an 8 GiB file on /mnt/data (sdb, priority 10). Because zram absorbs the first ~46 GiB this costs CPU and RAM rather than disk latency — but it is still memory the offload arena cannot have.

panels.title: Order≥9 free
panels.description: Free physically-contiguous memory in blocks of 2 MiB or larger, from /proc/buddyinfo. This is the ceiling on a PINNED host arena, and it collapses under fragmentation long before 'RAM available' looks alarming — when a pin fails despite plenty available, read this.

panels.title: CPU utilization by mode (%)
panels.description: Averaged across all cores and stacked to the total busy figure. 'system' dominating points at kernel work (page faults, DMA setup, copies); 'iowait' at storage; 'user' at compute.

panels.title: System memory breakdown
panels.description: Stacks to MemTotal. 'page cache' holds the NVMe-mmap'd PLE table, so it grows as that table is touched and is reclaimable; 'used' is anonymous/pinned and is not. Watch free approach zero while used climbs — that is the point swap starts.

panels.title: Locked / unevictable host memory
panels.description: Host pages the kernel cannot reclaim or swap. Mlocked counts mlock()'d pages; Unevictable is the superset that also covers driver-pinned pages. Which one a ROCm host arena lands in depends on the pinning path — read both, and treat the larger as the arena's true footprint.

panels.title: Swap traffic
panels.description: Bytes/s paged to and from swap (vmstat pswpin/pswpout x 4 KiB). Swap is zram-backed first, so this traffic is compression work against RAM, not NVMe I/O — it will NOT appear on the NVMe panels unless zram fills and the sdb swapfile takes over. Sustained bidirectional traffic still means host memory is oversubscribed and latency taken from that window is not comparable.

panels.title: Demand paging — major faults & NVMe reads
panels.description: Major faults are page faults that had to hit disk: for an NVMe-mmap'd weight or PLE table that is the read path itself, so a steady rate is normal and its size is the cost. Compare against NVMe bytes/s (right axis) to see the page amplification — bytes moved per fault.

panels.title: Pressure stall (PSI)
panels.description: Percent of wall time tasks were stalled waiting on a resource, from /proc/pressure. 'some' = at least one task stalled, 'full' = every runnable task stalled (memory only). This leads the utilization gauges: memory PSI rises while RAM used still looks fine, and full > 0 means the box is losing real throughput to reclaim.

panels.title: NVMe read
panels.description: Read throughput on the weight device — the NVMe holding the model weights and any mmap'd side tables (e.g. a PLE n-gram table), so it carries the weight-streaming traffic. The query pins device="nvme1n1"; edit that filter to whichever device backs the model store on this box. The OS device should stay near idle during a serve.

panels.title: NVMe read IOPS
panels.description: Completed read requests/s on the weight device. Read alongside 'Avg read size': the same throughput at 10x the IOPS means the access pattern fragmented, not that the device got busier.

panels.title: Avg read size
panels.description: Bytes per completed read = read_bytes / reads_completed. This is the prefetch signal: at ~4 KiB the device is servicing single-page demand faults one at a time; 128 KiB and up means readahead or the prefetch threads are coalescing. Low value with high IOPS is the pattern to fix.

panels.title: Read latency
panels.description: Average service time per read = read_time / reads_completed. Includes queueing, so it climbs under depth even when the device itself is fine — check it against queue depth before blaming the drive.

panels.title: Device busy
panels.description: Percent of wall time the weight device had at least one I/O in flight. Near 100% means the NVMe is the streaming bottleneck; well below it with poor throughput means the bottleneck is upstream (too few prefetch threads, or serialized faults).

panels.title: ARC hit ratio
panels.description: ZFS ARC hits / (hits + misses). The weight and PLE files are on ZFS, so ARC is the cache in front of the NVMe — a high ratio means most 'reads' never reach the device, and NVMe throughput understates real demand. ARC is capped well below the working set, so expect this to be low during streaming.

panels.title: NVMe throughput by device
panels.description: Read and write bytes/s per physical NVMe. The device holding the model weights and any mmap'd side tables is the weight-streaming one; the OS device should stay near idle during a serve. Writes on the weight device during a read-only serve are filesystem metadata or another job — worth explaining before trusting a read number.

panels.title: NVMe IOPS & queue depth
panels.description: Completed requests/s per device, with average queue depth on the right axis (io_time_weighted rate = mean requests in flight). Depth near 1 with high latency means requests are serialized — the streaming path is not issuing enough concurrency to fill the device.

panels.title: NVMe read latency & busy
panels.description: Average read service time per device (left, seconds) against device busy percent (right). Latency rising while busy is flat is queueing upstream; both rising together is genuine device saturation.

panels.title: Average read size (I/O granularity)
panels.description: Bytes per completed read, over time. Flat at ~4 KiB is page-at-a-time demand faulting — the worst case for streaming, since every page costs a full round trip. Steps upward mean readahead or prefetch threads are coalescing requests. This is the series to watch when tuning prefetch depth, not raw throughput.

panels.title: ZFS ARC — size vs cap, hit ratio
panels.description: ARC is the cache in front of the NVMe for the weight and PLE datasets, and it is host RAM the offload arena cannot use: ARC size counts as kernel memory, not page cache, so it inflates 'used' on the memory breakdown. Size pinned at the cap with a low hit ratio is the worst case — paying full RAM for a cache that is not absorbing the working set.

panels.title: Page amplification — NVMe bytes per major fault
panels.description: Bytes read from the weight device per 4 KiB major fault. 1.0 means each fault moved exactly its own page; higher means readahead pulled in more than was asked for — useful when it is prefetch, waste when it is not. The fault rate is floored at 1/s so that pread-thread traffic, which reaches the device without faulting, does not render as an infinite ratio.
